title: A Man with a Measuring Reed
sum: On the tenth day of the month, at the start of the year, in the twenty-fifth year of the exile, the hand of the LORD takes Ezekiel to the land of Israel, in visions, and sets him down on a very high mountain. A man who shines like bronze stands at a gate with a linen cord and a measuring reed. He tells the prophet to look, to listen and to remember everything, because he must report it to the house of Israel. Then the man measures. Gate after gate, court after court, he gives lengths and widths in a long cubit of about twenty inches.

The numbers are the message. After chapters of judgment, the last nine chapters of the book show a Temple whose walls and gates keep out what defiled the first one (chapter 8). The east gate is the first thing measured (40:6), because the glory of the LORD will return through it (43:1-5). The chapter names the priests who serve at the altar, the sons of Zadok (40:46).
readings: Read as a plan to be built

Some readers have taken the plan literally, as a blueprint that the returned exiles, or a later generation, should build. The detail (measurements, steps, tables, hooks) is the kind found in a builder's specification, and 43:10-11 tells Ezekiel to write the plan down so that Israel can "keep its whole design". On this reading the plan was never carried out when the Second Temple was built (see Ezra 3 and 6), and it waits for a future Temple.
Read as an ideal that was never meant to be built

Others read the plan as a vision of what the Temple should be, a program of restoration rather than a building contract. It is dated to the exile, it ignores the real hill (the mountain is "very high"), and its laws differ from the Torah's. On this reading its point is the holiness and presence it shows, not the stones (Jon Levenson's study of the program is the leading example).
Read as a picture fulfilled in Christ and the church

Christian writers from early on have read the Temple as the church or as Christ's body. Gregory the Great's homilies on Ezekiel take chapter 40 this way, and the New Testament speaks of the Temple as Jesus' body and the church (John 2:19-21; 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:19-22) and sees no temple in the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:22).

views.H: The vision is dated to 573 BC, the twenty-fifth year of the exile, fourteen years after the city fell (40:1), when the Temple had lain in ruins since its burning in 586 BC. The returned exiles built a Second Temple from about 520 BC on the old foundations and Solomon's pattern (Ezra 3:8-13; 6:3-5); they did not follow Ezekiel's plan, and no such building stood in history.
views.C: Scholars divide on whether chapters 40-42 are the prophet's own. Zimmerli saw a core of Ezekiel's vision, expanded by his school; others, such as Block, defend the visionary account as Ezekiel's own. The Hebrew of the measurements is badly damaged, and the Greek differs often (see the variants).
views.J: The sages valued the chapter and also feared it. The Talmud says the book of Ezekiel was nearly withdrawn because its words seemed to contradict the Torah, and that Hananiah son of Hezekiah, with three hundred jars of oil, explained them (Shabbat 13b). The Mishnah (Middot) gives the Second Temple's measurements, which differ from Ezekiel's in many ways (its altar, for example, is 32 cubits at the base). The Temple Scroll from Qumran has a quite different plan.
views.X: Early readers read it as Christ and the church: the church is the temple of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16). Reformed and Lutheran teaching treats the Old Testament Temple as fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 8-10), so that it is not rebuilt. Gregory the Great, honored in both the Catholic and Orthodox churches, read the Temple as the church.
views.F: For dispensational readers the Temple is a literal Temple of the future millennial kingdom (Scofield; Walvoord, Pentecost). Some Orthodox Jewish readers expect a Third Temple built by the Messiah, though they do not agree that Ezekiel's plan is its blueprint.

deep.h: Which witnesses were read for this part
deep.b: For chapters 40 to 43 the Hebrew text was read from the Leningrad Codex with its word-by-word glosses, together with the machine-found Ketiv and Qere notes. The Dead Sea Scrolls were read in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription: the only Ezekiel scroll that preserves any of these chapters is 4QEzek-a (4Q73), at 41:3-6, and there it agrees with the Masoretic Text where it is preserved. The Greek was read as printed in Swete's edition of Codex Vaticanus, so that where the notes and variants of these four chapters say "the Greek" they mean that text.

deep.h: The whole Temple at a glance
deep.b:
All figures are in the long cubit of 40:5 (about 52 cm). The Hebrew numbers are uncertain in several places; the variants and notes say where. The table follows the Plain of chapters 40 to 43 (the altar is in 43:13-17). Each part is listed once: the house and the separate area behind it are separate rows, so their lengths are not counted twice.

One way to add up the east-west parts, which the text does not do itself: outer gate 50, outer court 100, inner gate 50, inner court 100, house 100, separate area and back building 100, a total of 500. That is the size of the walled square in 42:20 if its unit is cubits, which would favor cubits over the Hebrew's reeds in 42:16-19. In 45:2 the Hebrew again gives 500 by 500 with no unit.

Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 6-7): the main hall (40 cubits) and innermost room (20 cubits) have the same number of cubits as Ezekiel's, though Ezekiel's cubit is the long one (40:5), so the rooms are not the same size in feet. Both temples have carved cherubim and palm trees (1 Kings 6:29; Ezekiel 41:18-20). Solomon's porch was twenty cubits across and ten deep (1 Kings 6:3); Ezekiel's is twenty across and eleven deep. Solomon's side rooms are 5, 6 and 7 cubits wide; Ezekiel's are 4. Solomon's furnishings included ten lampstands (1 Kings 7:49), ten bronze basins and the bronze Sea (1 Kings 7:23-39), a table for the bread of the presence (1 Kings 7:48; 2 Chronicles 4:8 speaks of ten tables) and the ark (1 Kings 8:6); these chapters mention none of them. The Tabernacle had a court of 100 by 50 cubits (Exodus 27:9-18); Ezekiel's inner court is 100 by 100. The Second Temple was built to Cyrus's order at 60 cubits high and 60 wide (Ezra 6:3); the Mishnah describes it in tractate Middot. The Temple Scroll from Qumran (11QT) lays out three concentric courts, a plan that differs from Ezekiel's (see Yadin's edition).

echoes: Ezekiel 1:1-3; Ezekiel 8:1-4; Ezekiel 28:14; Isaiah 2:2-3; Micah 4:1-2; 1 Kings 6-7; Exodus 25-40; Zechariah 2:1-5; Revelation 11:1; Revelation 21:9-22:5

settings.what: The vision of the new Temple (chapters 40-43, the first half of the vision)
settings.by: Ezekiel, reporting what a heavenly guide showed and said to him
settings.to: The exiles of Judah in Babylonia, and above all those who sat before him; later, the people of the Second Temple who read the collected book
settings.when: The twenty-fifth year of the exile (about 573 BC), fourteen years after the fall of Jerusalem, on the tenth of the month; the last dated vision in the book
settings.why: For people who had lost Temple, land and king, the vision answered two questions: whether the LORD would live among them again, and what would keep the next Temple from being defiled as the first had been (chapter 8). The measurements, walls and gates make the answer visible. Knowing the audience changes how the numbers read: they are a promise to people who had no Temple to stand in.
settings.readers: The people who rebuilt the Temple after 538 BC did not use this plan, and later readers, in the age of the Second Temple and after its destruction in AD 70, read it as a promise, a puzzle or a program.
views: A plan for a Temple to be built
The text commands Ezekiel to write the plan so that Israel "keep its whole design" (43:11), and the vision's details look like a plan for builders.
An ideal vision
The plan was never built and cannot be: it sets the Temple on a mountain, the river in 47 flows from it, and the land is divided in equal strips. It speaks of a renewed Israel rather than a building.
A picture of the church or of the world to come
Christian readers see the Temple as the church (Gregory the Great) or as the new creation, as in Revelation 21-22.

settings.what: The measuring of the gates, courts and porch
settings.by: The guide, with Ezekiel looking on
settings.to: Ezekiel, who must tell the house of Israel (40:4)
settings.when: During the vision of 573 BC, as the guide leads him through the east, north and south gates
settings.why: The tour begins at the boundary. A Temple whose wall, gates and chambers are measured first is a Temple built to keep the holy and the ordinary apart (42:20). The gates are also the places where people are checked, where offerings are slaughtered, and where the glory will enter (43:1-4).
views: A literal plan
The measurements are the plan of a real building.
A literary ideal
The repeated measurements (the gates are copied three times) read as a deliberate pattern of order and balance, not a drawing.

title: The Great Hall, the Most Holy Place and the Carved Walls
sum: The guide takes the prophet to the house itself. He measures the porch pillars, the great hall (forty cubits by twenty), and then goes alone into the innermost room, a perfect cube of twenty cubits: "This is the most holy place." The prophet does not go in. The chapter moves outward again: the side rooms in three stories, the building at the back, the paneling and the closed windows.

The carvings are the heart of the chapter: cherubim with two faces, a human and a young lion, between palm trees, all around the walls. The text does not say what is in the innermost room. There is no ark and no mercy seat. A wooden altar, called "the table that is before the LORD", stands in front. The Hebrew of this chapter is among the hardest in the book, and the Plain says so where it must.
readings: The hall and inner room have Solomon's proportions (1 Kings 6:2, 17, 20), and the carved cherubim and palm trees are the same as the old Temple's (1 Kings 6:29). The vision is what the first Temple was meant to be.
With palm trees, cherubim and a river to come (47:1-12), the house is the garden of God (28:13-14; 31:8-9). The cherubim guard, as in Genesis 3:24, and the LORD dwells with people again.

views.H: The side rooms, the porch, the carved cherubim and palms and the folding doors are the details of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 6), which Ezekiel, a priest's son, knew from his youth in Jerusalem. The first Temple was far away from where he sat, and had been burned in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9).
views.C: The Hebrew of 41:6-26 has many rare words and breaks (41:21 stops in the middle), and the Greek differs. Scholars debate how much of the detail is due to later hands. One of the Dead Sea copies, 4QEzek-a (4Q73), preserves parts of 41:3-6 and agrees with the Masoretic Text there, including twenty cubits for the innermost room in 41:4, where the Greek has forty.
views.J: The sages treated the Temple's measurements as practical law. Tractate Middot in the Mishnah records the measurements of the Second Temple, and the Jewish tradition of the Third Temple (see 43:5) takes some details from Ezekiel and some from the Mishnah.
views.X: For readers who take the Temple as Christ and the church, the innermost room points to the presence of God with people (Hebrews 9:11-12; Revelation 21:3). The empty innermost room is read as a sign that the LORD's own presence fills it.
views.F: Dispensational readers see these walls as the walls of a Temple of the coming kingdom; others see the carved garden as the new creation.

deep.b: The great hall (40 by 20) and innermost room (20 by 20) have the same number of cubits as Solomon's (1 Kings 6:17, 20), though Ezekiel's cubit is the long one. The carved cherubim and palm trees run all around, as in 1 Kings 6:29. The doors folded on pivots (1 Kings 6:34). The side rooms rise in three stories and rest on supports that do not cut into the wall (1 Kings 6:5-6). The differences are as telling. Ezekiel's cherubim have two faces, a human and a young lion (41:18-19), where 1 Kings 6:29 says nothing of faces; his side rooms are four cubits wide, not five, six and seven; and where Solomon had an ark and two large cherubim in the innermost room (1 Kings 6:23-28; 8:6), Ezekiel gives the room only its size. Solomon's hall had ten lampstands (1 Kings 7:49) and a table for the bread (1 Kings 7:48; 2 Chronicles 4:8 speaks of ten tables), and Ezekiel's has a single wooden altar-table (41:22).

echoes: 1 Kings 6:2-38; 1 Kings 7:48-49; 2 Chronicles 4:8; Exodus 26:33-34; Leviticus 16:2; Ezekiel 10:1-22; Ezekiel 28:13-14; Genesis 3:24; Hebrews 9:1-12

settings.to: Ezekiel, to be reported to the exiles
settings.when: In the same vision of 573 BC, after the courts have been measured
settings.why: The house is the center of the whole plan, and its holiness is shown by its silence: the guide goes into the innermost room alone, the prophet waits, and nothing inside is described. For priests' sons in exile who had no Temple to enter, the empty cube said that the LORD's holiness was greater than what the old Temple's furniture had held.
views: The empty room means the LORD alone fills it
Some readers see the lack of the ark as intentional, a sign that the LORD himself, not an object, is present (Jeremiah 3:16-17).
The description is simply partial
Others note that the vision describes only the building and its dimensions here, and that the ark is not explicitly excluded.

title: The Priests' Rooms and the Wall Around the Holy Area
sum: The guide leads Ezekiel out to the north rooms, a block of three-story chambers a hundred cubits long and fifty wide, with a matching block on the south. He explains their use: there the priests eat the most holy offerings and lay them down, and there they change their clothes before they go out among the people. Holiness, in this chapter, can spread, and must be kept from spreading to the wrong places.

Then the guide takes him out the east gate and measures the whole area on all four sides, five hundred in each direction, and a wall that exists "to separate the holy from the ordinary". In the Hebrew the count is five hundred reeds, not cubits, and the Plain follows it, with a variant. This wall is the answer to chapter 8 and 43:8, where the first Temple stood next to the king's house with only a wall between.
readings: Read as a manual for priests
The chapter answers a practical question: where do the priests eat, store and change? Leviticus told them to eat their share in a holy place (Leviticus 6:16, 26), and this is the place.
Read as a map of holiness
The rooms, the clothes and the wall make a gradient from the most holy to the ordinary. The chapter shows how the Temple area is graded, and its center is the house.

views.H: The complex of rooms matches the storerooms and priests' chambers of the first and second Temples (Jeremiah 36:10; Nehemiah 13:4-9), and the 500-cubit enclosure matches the size the Mishnah gives to the Second Temple's mount (Middot 2:1).
views.C: The plan of the rooms in 42:3-12 is so obscure that no reconstruction has won general agreement, and the Greek is shorter. The rule about changing clothes (42:14) is repeated in 44:19 and 46:20, which some scholars see as part of the same layer.
views.J: The rule that priests eat the most holy things in a holy place follows the Torah (Leviticus 6:16, 26). The Mishnah lists the Second Temple's chambers (Middot 5), which are not Ezekiel's.
views.X: Christian writers have read the rooms and wall as the order of the church, and the separation of the holy from the ordinary as the call to holiness (1 Peter 2:9).
views.F: For readers who expect a literal future Temple, the rooms are for the priests of the age to come.

echoes: Leviticus 6:16-29; Leviticus 10:10; Leviticus 16:23-24; Ezekiel 44:19; Ezekiel 46:19-20; Nehemiah 13:4-9; Jeremiah 36:10

settings.what: The priests' rooms and their rules
settings.to: Ezekiel; the rules are for the priests of Zadok's line (40:46; 43:19), and through Ezekiel for the exiles
settings.when: In the vision of 573 BC, after the house has been measured
settings.why: The priests had failed to tell the holy from the ordinary (22:26). These rooms give them places that do it for them: a holy place to eat the most holy things, and a place to put on and off the clothes of service, so that holiness is not carried out to the people.
views: A rule to protect the people
Holy things could be dangerous to those who had not been prepared for them.
A rule to protect the holy things
The priest's service clothes are themselves holy and must not be treated like everyday clothes.

settings.what: The measuring of the whole holy area
settings.when: As the vision tour of 573 BC finishes the inside and goes out by the east gate
settings.why: The final measure closes the plan with a boundary: a wall that marks the holy off from the ordinary. For the exiles it recalled the failure of chapter 8 and 43:8, where unclean things stood near the Temple, and promised a place where that could not happen.

title: The Glory Comes Back
sum: The guide leads Ezekiel to the east gate. There the glory of the God of Israel is coming from the east, with a sound like many waters, and the earth lights up. It is the same sight he saw at the Kebar canal and in the Temple before the destruction, and he falls on his face. The glory enters the house by the east gate, the way it had left, and fills the house. This is the high point of the book.

A voice from the house tells him that this is the place of the LORD's throne, where he will live among the Israelites forever, and that they will never again defile his name. Ezekiel is to describe the house to Israel so that they are ashamed and keep its design. The chapter ends with the altar, measured stage by stage, and seven days of offerings to make it ready. On the eighth day the priests will offer the people's offerings, and the LORD says: "I will accept you."
readings: Read as the end of the exile
The glory left in 10-11; now it returns. The LORD's absence is over, and the exiles are told that what ended in 586 BC was not the last word.
Read as the beginning of the new world

The glory fills the house as it filled the Tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-35) and Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 8:10-11), and John sees no temple in the new Jerusalem because the glory of God lights it (Revelation 21:22-23).

views.H: The returned exiles built a Temple, but the sources do not say that the glory filled it as it filled Solomon's (Ezra 6:16-18; Haggai 2:7-9 looks forward to a glory still to come). The rabbis counted the glory (Shekhinah) among five things the Second Temple lacked (Yoma 21b).
views.C: Many scholars see 43:1-12 as the climax of the whole book, tied to 1-3 and 8-11 by repeated words (43:3). The speech of 43:7-9 is sometimes seen as a later expansion, and the Greek is shorter at 43:10-11. The altar measures (43:13-17) are very difficult in the Hebrew.
views.J: Jewish tradition holds that the glory left the Temple in ten stages (Rosh Hashanah 31a) and that the Second Temple lacked it (Yoma 21b). The return of the glory is therefore the hope of a Temple to come, not a past event.
views.X: Christian readers see the glory returning in Jesus (John 1:14; 2:19-21) and in the church (1 Corinthians 3:16-17), and the new Jerusalem as the final return (Revelation 21:3, 22-23).
views.F: For readers who expect a literal Temple in a future kingdom, 43:1-12 is the return of the glory at that Temple; they take 43:18-27 as the altar's dedication.

deep.h: The glory's journey through the book
deep.b: The glory is the book's thread. It appears at the Kebar canal (1:28; 3:12, 23); is in the Temple (8:4); goes up from the cherub to the threshold (9:3; 10:4); stands at the east gate (10:18-19); goes up from the city to the mountain east of it (11:22-23). It comes back from the east (43:2), enters by the east gate (43:4) and fills the house (43:5). After this the east gate is shut because the LORD entered by it (44:1-3), the glory is seen again in 44:4, and the city is named "The LORD Is There" (48:35). The direction is the key: the glory left toward the east and returns from the east. The rabbis described the departure in ten stages (Rosh Hashanah 31a).

The altar is where the people meet the LORD. It is placed in the inner court, in front of the house (40:47), and its dedication takes seven days (43:25-26), as the Tabernacle's did (Exodus 29:35-37) and as the people's feasts do. After it is ready, the offerings of the people can be accepted (43:27). The chapter's last words, "I will accept you", repeat the promise of 20:40-41.

echoes: Ezekiel 1:28; Ezekiel 3:12, 23; Ezekiel 8:4; Ezekiel 10:18-19; Ezekiel 11:22-23; Ezekiel 20:40-41; Ezekiel 44:1-4; Ezekiel 48:35; Exodus 40:34-35; 1 Kings 8:10-11; Isaiah 60:1-2; Haggai 2:7-9; Zechariah 14:4; John 1:14; Revelation 21:22-23

settings.what: The return of the glory, and the LORD's word from the house
settings.by: The glory of the LORD; a voice from the house (43:6-7); the guide stands at Ezekiel's side
settings.to: Ezekiel, "son of man", to be told to the house of Israel
settings.when: In the vision of 573 BC, at the east gate, at the end of the tour of the outer and inner courts
settings.why: For exiles who had been told that the LORD had left (chapters 10-11) and that their kings and their idols had driven him out, the word is that he will come back, will live among them, and will not leave again if they keep the house holy. The prophet is to show them the house so that they feel shame, and the shame is meant to lead to keeping its "rules".
views: The return is a promise of the future
The Temple was not rebuilt this way, and the glory has not yet returned in the way described.
The return is fulfilled in Christ and the church
The glory has already come in Jesus (John 1:14), and the Temple is now his body and the church.

settings.to: Ezekiel, for the exiles and the priests who would serve
settings.when: In the vision of 573 BC, after the LORD has spoken from the house
settings.why: The altar is measured last, after the glory has filled the house, because it is the place of service. The numbers are the numbers of a stepped altar, probably four tiers, in a square.

settings.what: The rules for making the altar ready
settings.by: The Lord GOD, through the guide
settings.to: Ezekiel, who is told "you" will give the bull; the rules bind the priests of Zadok's line, who serve at the altar (40:46; 43:19)
settings.when: The day the altar is made, and seven days after; then on the eighth day offerings begin
settings.why: A new altar must be cleansed from sin and consecrated before it can be used. The rules answer the problem of an altar that is unclean from the start, as the old Temple had been (chapter 8), by seven days of sin offerings, burnt offerings and atonement. The rules differ in some details from Moses's law for the Tabernacle (Exodus 29:35-37; Leviticus 8:14-17).
views: The rules differ from Moses's, and this is a problem
The sages worried that Ezekiel's laws conflicted with the Torah (Shabbat 13b), and the harmonizing is old.
The rules are the LORD's new rules for a new Temple
Some scholars see Ezekiel as a prophet who could give new rules, as Moses did.

traditions.q: Will animal sacrifices be offered again, as in Ezekiel 43:18-27? (The book-level card on the Temple of Ezekiel 40-48 sets out the wider question. Postmillennial, historic premillennial and Anabaptist readings are not set out here.)
views: Dispensationalist

Yes, in a future Temple in the kingdom age. The usual dispensational reading takes the offerings as memorials that look back to the cross (the Scofield Reference Bible's notes on Ezekiel 40-48; Walvoord, The Millennial Kingdom), and Pentecost (Things to Come) also expects a future Temple. John Whitcomb, a dispensationalist, argues against the memorial reading in "Christ's Atonement and Animal Sacrifices in Israel" (Grace Theological Journal 6, 1985): the offerings will not be primarily memorial, and Ezekiel's own word "atonement" (45:15, 17, 20) means a ceremonial cleansing that keeps Israel in right order with the LORD in his Temple, not a removal of spiritual guilt.
scofield
walvoord-millennial
pentecost-things
whitcomb-sacrifices-gtj
Reformed

No. The sacrifices of the law were shadows of Christ's single sacrifice (Hebrews 10:1-18) and ended in him. The Westminster Confession (chapter 19) teaches that the ceremonial laws are abrogated under the New Testament. Amillennial writers such as Hoekema read Ezekiel 40-48 as a symbolic picture of God's people and the new earth. Not every Reformed Christian is amillennial.
westminster
hoekema-future
Baptist

No further sacrifices for sin. The Second London Confession (1689, chapter 19) repeats the Westminster teaching that the ceremonial laws have been abrogated by Christ. The confession does not speak of Ezekiel 40-48 or of a millennial Temple.
london-1689
Anglican

No further sacrifices for sin. The Thirty-Nine Articles say that Christ's offering once made on the cross is the perfect redemption, propitiation and satisfaction for all sin, and that there is no other (Article 31); and that the ceremonies and rites of the law given by Moses do not bind Christian people (Article 7). They do not speak of Ezekiel 40-48.
thirty-nine-articles
Lutheran

No. The Augsburg Confession (article 17) rejects the opinion that the godly will take possession of an earthly kingdom before the resurrection of the dead, and its Apology (article 24) teaches that Christ's death is the one sacrifice that makes satisfaction for sin.
augsburg
apology-augsburg
Catholic

No further bloody sacrifice. The one sacrifice of Christ on the cross is made present in the Eucharist, which the Church calls a sacrifice (Catechism of the Catholic Church 1366). The Catechism rejects even modified forms of millenarianism, the hope of an earthly kingdom within history (676), and calls the Church "especially, the holy temple" (756).
ccc
Orthodox

No Orthodox council has ruled on the meaning of Ezekiel 40-48 or on whether sacrifices will return. The Divine Liturgy of John Chrysostom speaks of a "bloodless" service of worship; that is the church's language of worship, not a ruling on this question.
liturgy-chrysostom
